q: How is the -er at the end of parler said?
o: Like the er in English her
why: Final -er sounds ay in French: parler sounds like pahr-lay.

q: Which final letter is usually SOUNDED in French?
why: c, r, f and l (careful) are usually sounded; most other final consonants are silent.

q: What does a capital N mean in the pronunciation line?
o: Say the vowel through the nose, without the n
why: N marks a nasal vowel: the n itself is not pronounced.

q: Who do you call vous?
o: A shop assistant you don't know
why: vous is for strangers, staff and anyone older, and for more than one person.

q: Why is it bonne in Bonne journée?
o: journée is feminine, so good takes its feminine form
bonne is used only at night
why: journée is a feminine word, and bon changes to bonne to agree with it.

q: How do you say please to a friend?
why: With tu people (friends, family), please is s'il te plaît.

q: What is the best way to remember if a noun is masculine or feminine?
o: Guess from what the thing is
Learn every noun with its article
All nouns ending in -e are feminine
Use le when you are not sure
why: The gender of most nouns can't be guessed, so learn each one with le, la, un or une.

q: appartement is masculine. How do you say the apartment?
why: Before a vowel, le becomes l': l'appartement.

q: How do you usually hear that a French noun is plural?
o: From the article in front, like les or des
You can't hear it at all
why: The plural -s is silent, so the article (les, des) tells you.

q: I'm twenty-five =
why: Age uses avoir plus ans: I have twenty-five years.

q: Which subject goes with sont?
why: sont is the they form of être: ils sont, elles sont.

q: Why is it j'ai and not je ai?
o: je drops its e before a vowel
why: Elision: je becomes j' before a vowel.

q: Who's hungry? Me! In French, Me! is:
why: A pronoun standing alone is a stress pronoun: moi.

q: What does on est usually mean in conversation?
why: on is the everyday we, with the il form of the verb: on est.

q: with them (two women) =
why: After avec, use a stress pronoun; for women it is elles.

q: Where does a color go in French?
o: At the end of the sentence
why: Colors go after the noun: une robe rouge.

q: Why is it une robe blanche but un pull blanc?
o: robe is feminine, so the adjective takes its feminine form
why: The adjective agrees with the noun: robe is feminine, pull is masculine.

q: Which adjective goes BEFORE the noun?
why: petit is one of the short group (petit, grand, bon, beau, nouveau, jeune, vieux) that go first.

q: Which three endings sound exactly the same?
why: -e, -es and -ent are silent, so parle, parles and parlent sound alike.

q: I'm speaking =
why: The French present covers -ing: je parle.

q: nous + manger =
why: manger keeps its e before -ons to keep the soft g: mangeons.

q: Where do ne and pas go?
o: ne before the verb, pas after it
Both at the end of the sentence
pas before the verb, ne after it
why: ne … pas wraps the conjugated verb: je ne parle pas.

q: I don't have a cat =
why: After a negative verb, un becomes de: pas de chat.

q: Je ne suis jamais en retard means:
why: ne … jamais = never.

q: How do you turn Tu parles français into a question with est-ce que?
why: est-ce que goes at the very start; the rest of the sentence stays the same.

q: ville (town) is feminine. Which town? =
why: quel agrees with its noun: ville is feminine singular, so quelle.

q: Which word means where?
why: où with an accent means where; ou without it means or.

q: He's a teacher (professeur) =
why: After il est, a job takes no article.

q: il y a means:
why: il y a = there is and there are, for one thing or many.

q: Which sentence is correct?
why: c'est goes with a noun and its article: c'est un musée.

q: How do you say his mother (Lucas's mother)?
why: The possessive agrees with mère, which is feminine: sa mère, even though Lucas is a man.

q: Why is it mon amie and not ma amie?
o: Before a vowel sound, ma becomes mon
why: French avoids two vowels side by side, so ma becomes mon before a vowel, even with a feminine noun.

q: Which word goes before hôtel (masculine, silent h)?
why: Before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or a silent h, ce becomes cet: cet hôtel.

q: How do you say 75?
why: 75 is sixty plus fifteen: soixante-quinze.

q: What does Il est vingt heures mean?
why: Schedules use the 24-hour clock: vingt heures is 8 p.m.

q: How do you say May 1?
why: Day before month, and the first is le premier.

q: How do you say I'd like some water?
why: eau starts with a vowel, so some is de l': de l'eau.

q: Which sentence is about coffee in general?
why: After aimer, French uses le for the thing in general: j'aime le café.

q: What does du become after ne … pas?
why: After a negative, the partitive becomes de: il n'y a pas de pain.

q: Why is je voudrais better than je veux with a server?
o: je voudrais is softer; je veux sounds blunt
je voudrais is only for food
je veux is the vous form
why: Both are correct French, but je voudrais (I'd like) is the polite way to ask.

q: What should you say before asking anything in a shop?
why: In France you always say bonjour before a request; salut is only for friends.

q: How do you begin Could you…? to a stranger?
why: To a stranger use vous, and its ending is -iez: vous pourriez.

q: Which is right for a city?
why: Cities take plain à: à Paris.

q: What does à + le become?
why: à + le always contracts to au.

q: How do you say in Japan (le Japon is masculine)?
why: A masculine country takes au: au Japon.

q: How do you say The weather's nice?
why: Weather uses faire: il fait beau.

q: Which is the ils form of aller?
why: aller is irregular: ils vont.

q: What does Je viens de Boston mean?
why: venir de + a city says where you come from.

q: Which is right?
why: After vouloir, the second verb stays in the infinitive, with nothing in between.

q: I can swim, meaning I know how to:
why: A skill you've learned uses savoir: je sais nager.

q: What is the vous form of pouvoir?
why: pouvoir with vous is pouvez.

q: How do you say I'm going to eat?
why: aller + the infinitive, with nothing in between.

q: Where does ne … pas go in the futur proche?
o: Around vais: Je ne vais pas partir.
Around partir: Je vais ne partir pas.
Before je: Ne pas je vais partir.
At the end: Je vais partir ne pas.
why: ne … pas wraps around the conjugated verb, aller.

q: What does Il va pleuvoir mean?
why: va + pleuvoir: the near future, it's going to rain.

q: Which is right?
why: se lever needs its pronoun, and with je it is me.

q: Which reflexive pronoun goes with nous?
why: With nous, the reflexive pronoun is nous too: nous nous levons.

q: How do you say I'm going to go to bed?
why: The pronoun goes before the infinitive and matches je: je vais me coucher.

q: A stranger asks you the way. How do you tell them 'Turn right'?
why: A stranger gets the vous form: Tournez à droite.

q: How do you say 'Look!' to a friend?
why: -er verbs drop the -s in a tu command: Regarde!

q: What does Il faut partir mean?
o: He has to go, but nobody else does.
why: il faut + infinitive says something is necessary; this il is not 'he'.

q: Which is correct for 'I went to Paris'?
why: aller takes être in the passé composé: je suis allé.

q: Léa went out last night. Which is right?
why: sortir takes être, and the participle agrees with Léa: sortie.

q: Where does ne … pas go in the passé composé?
o: Around the helper verb: Je n'ai pas mangé.
Around the participle: J'ai ne mangé pas.
Before everything: Ne j'ai pas mangé.
After the participle: J'ai mangé ne pas.
why: ne … pas wraps the helper verb, the part that is conjugated.

q: Which word means 'or'?
why: ou with no accent is or; où with an accent is where.

q: Your friend asks Pourquoi? How does your answer start?
why: parce que gives the reason that answers pourquoi.

q: In et un café, is the t of et pronounced?
o: Yes, it links like the s in les amis
No, never: et and un stay apart
why: The t of et is never pronounced, even before a vowel.

q: You hear Je sais pas. What does it mean?
why: Spoken French drops ne; pas still makes it negative.

q: Which verb form goes with on?
why: on takes the il form, even when it means we.

q: A friend says On va au cinéma? What do they mean?
o: Shall we go to the movies?
One must go to the movies.
why: on is the everyday we, and a rising voice makes it a question.

q: Which ending goes with ils in the imparfait?
why: ils takes -aient: ils parlaient. It sounds like -ais and -ait.

q: Il pleuvait quand je suis arrivé. Why is pleuvait in the imparfait?
o: It's the background: what was going on
It happened once and was over
why: The rain is the scene; the arrival is the event, in the passé composé.

q: How do you say 'When I was little'?
why: A description of how things were takes the imparfait: j'étais.

q: How do you say 'I'll work'?
why: Infinitive + -ai for je: je travaillerai.

q: 'When I'm in Paris, I'll visit the Louvre.' Which is right?
why: After quand, French uses the future when the time is in the future: je serai.

q: What is the future stem of être?
why: être has the future stem ser-: je serai, tu seras.

q: You're holding a jacket (la veste). 'I'll take it' =
why: veste is feminine, so it's la, and it goes before the verb.

q: Which pronoun means 'to her'?
why: Verbs with à take lui for to him or to her.

q: A server asks Vous voulez du café? How do you say 'Yes, I'd like some'?
why: en replaces du + noun and goes before the verb: j'en voudrais.

q: 'My sister is taller than me.' Which is right?
why: plus … que, grande agrees with sœur, and moi follows que.

q: 'This bread is better.' =
why: bon becomes meilleur; never plus bon.

q: Which word goes with a verb: 'She sings better'?
why: With a verb, better is mieux: Elle chante mieux.

q: How do you say 'the movie I saw'?
why: j' is the subject of the next verb, so que, and French never drops it.

q: Which word goes in: un ami ___ habite à Lyon?
why: The next word is a verb, habite, so qui.

q: la ville ___ j'habite =
why: A place, where: où, with its accent.
